items.title: Canada Packers posts Q3 loss amid ‘sharp and unusual’ market deterioration
items.description: A confluence of unusual headwinds from weaker demand to plummeting hog prices weighed on pork producer Canada Packers Inc.’s third-quarter results.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Pork chops are seen in the meat counter of a grocery store in Montreal, on Thursday, April 30, 2020. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Paul Chiasson]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Paul Chiasson</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: A confluence of unusual headwinds from weaker demand to plummeting hog prices weighed on pork producer Canada Packers Inc.’s third-quarter results.
items.body:
MISSISSAUGA — A confluence of unusual headwinds from weaker demand to plummeting hog prices weighed on pork producer Canada Packers Inc.’s third-quarter results.

Chief executive Dennis Organ said the company’s losses extended into the third quarter as it contended with “the combination of softer U.S. demand, slower exports and high year-over-year U.S. inventories at a time of steady supply.”

But Organ said the downturn is “cyclical.”

“The reason I consider it cyclical, one is: I’ve seen it before multiple times. Two, it’s the relationship between demand and supply, which happens in all businesses,” he told analysts during an earnings call on Wednesday.

  • Latest updates on company news here

While Organ said he remains confident on a recovery, he said he has “no idea” when the market will return to normal.

The Mississauga, Ont.-based pork producer reported a loss of $28.1 million or 94 cents per diluted share in the quarter ended Sept. 26 compared with a profit of $25.6 million or 86 cents per diluted share a year earlier.

The results included a $47.6 million non-cash decrease in fair value of biological assets compared with $4.9 million in the same quarter last year. On an adjusted basis, it earned 23 cents per share in its latest quarter compared with an adjusted profit of $1.13 per share a year earlier.

RBC analyst Irene Nattel said Canada Packers’ soft earnings were in line with expectations, reflecting a “sharp deterioration in market conditions and the absence of typical seasonal profitability dynamics, driving margin compression.”

Lower pork cut-out, which estimates the value of a hog based on the prices for each individual cut of meat from the animal, also weighed on overall sales, the company said.

“Cut-out values declined approximately 15 per cent from a year ago, and the weakness we experienced in the second quarter continued through the third quarter,” Organ said.

Wholesale commodity prices for hogs have plunged to a five-year low to roughly US$62 per pound, which also added volatility to the company’s financial results.

“While we can’t control commodity markets, our attention remains squarely on how we operate,” Organ said.

Sales in the quarter totalled $420.7 million, down from $481.8 million a year ago, when they included operations not acquired in its spinoff from Maple Leaf Foods Inc.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 28, 2026.

items._ogDesc: U.S. President Donald Trump drew criticism Wednesday for celebrating election victories by a Quebec separatist and a British Columbia Conservative, days after his administration accused Canadian politicians of interfering in U.S. elections.
items.body:
TORONTO — U.S. President Donald Trump drew criticism Wednesday for celebrating election victories by a Quebec separatist and a British Columbia Conservative, days after his administration accused Canadian politicians of interfering in U.S. elections.

With U.S. midterm elections approaching, Trump shared an article portraying the Quebec victory as a setback for Prime Minister Mark Carney and hailed the Conservative win in British Columbia as evidence of the party’s growing strength.

But neither election was a referendum on Carney, whose federal Liberal Party is separate from British Columbia’s provincial Conservatives. Analysts say both results reflected provincial politics, not declining support for the prime minister.

“Congratulations to Paul St-Pierre Plamondon on his WIN!” Trump wrote Tuesday on Truth Social, more than three weeks after the Quebec separatist leader’s Oct. 5 election victory. Trump linked to an article headlined “Separatists win Quebec provincial election in blow to Mark Carney.”

Trump also congratulated British Columbia’s premier-designate, Lorne Doerkson, on his “Big Victory,” adding: “Conservatives are moving strong in Canada!” The post came one minute before his congratulations to Quebec’s separatist leader.

The posts come amid Trump’s trade war and repeated threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state. St-Pierre Plamondon has criticized Trump’s tariffs and ruled out holding a Quebec independence referendum while Trump remains president.

Trump’s trade war with Canada has become an issue in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, particularly in Michigan and Maine, where Republican candidates have faced pressure over tariffs hurting local businesses. Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers has called for an end to the tariff war.

“It is highly unusual for a U.S. President to comment on Canadian provincial politics or to congratulate provincial election winners,” said Daniel Béland, a political science professor at McGill University in Montreal.

Béland said neither result should be interpreted as a rejection of Carney, whose popularity has been bolstered by his response to Trump.

Nelson Wiseman, a University of Toronto political scientist, said Trump misunderstands Canada’s Conservatives, noting that Doerkson has criticized Trump’s tariffs and called him a bully.

Doerkson spoke with Carney on Tuesday, with both leaders emphasizing cooperation on economic growth and investment.

“Carney’s popularity is at a stratospheric level,” Wiseman said. “The more Trump attacks Canada and Carney, the more popular Carney becomes.”

The U.S. Embassy in Ottawa last week accused Canadian politicians of seeking to influence the Nov. 3 midterms. It cited Industry Minister Mélanie Joly’s comments about targeting Republican states with retaliatory tariffs and Ontario Premier Doug Ford’s U.S. advertisement featuring former President Ronald Reagan criticizing tariffs.

The embassy also cited 11 Canadians charged with illegally voting in U.S. elections between 2012 and 2026, without linking the cases to the Canadian government.

Carney rejected the allegations, saying they had “no merit,” and expressed disappointment with U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra.

Asked Wednesday whether the Trump administration was setting up Canada to be the fall guy if Republicans suffer heavy losses in the U.S. midterms, Carney laughed.

“That’s an interesting way of framing it,” Carney said, before adding that Canada would pursue a trade deal with Washington only when it served Canadian interests.

Beland warned that the accusations could foreshadow a “Blame Canada” narrative if Republicans suffer losses in the midterms.

“It is absurd for President Trump to comment on Canadian provincial politics while the U.S. embassy in Canada is falsely claiming that country is interfering in the U.S. midterms,” Beland said.

Rob Gillies, The Associated Press

items.body:
OTTAWA — Industry Minister Mélanie Joly says Ottawa is consulting its lawyers about remarks by Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. chief executive Lourenco Goncalves suggesting he bought Stelco to protect his company’s U.S. operations from Canadian competition.

She says the federal government is examining the potential legal implications of his comments as the U.S.-based owner of Stelco faces a deadline to demonstrate how it will honour job commitments at its Ontario steel mills.

She says Goncalves’ “confessions” during a televised interview Tuesday could influence Ottawa’s ongoing enforcement action.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

In an interview with CBC News, Goncalves says he bought Stelco because the Canadian company was flooding the U.S. market with steel and undercutting prices.

He also told Power & Politics host David Cochrane that he intends to sell the company in about a year now that he is what he called “persona non grata” in Canada.

Cleveland-Cliffs announced plans on Sept. 28 to lay off up to 500 workers at Stelco’s Hamilton Works and Lake Erie Works in Nanticoke, Ont., blaming U.S. tariffs, weak demand and an oversupply of imported steel in Canada.

items.title: ‘Now or maybe never’: Cabinet ministers skeptical Trump can compromise, sources say
items.description: Cabinet ministers briefed on the increased pace of talks between Canada and the United States remain skeptical U.S. President Donald Trump will make the necessary concessions to secure a deal. However, many who spoke to CTV News are convinced he wants one.

items._ogDesc: Cabinet ministers briefed on the increased pace of talks between Canada and the United States remain skeptical U.S. President Donald Trump will make the necessary concessions to secure a deal. However, many who spoke to CTV News are convinced he wants one.
items.body:
Cabinet ministers briefed on the increased pace of talks between Canada and the United States remain skeptical U.S. President Donald Trump will make the necessary concessions to secure a deal. However, many who spoke to CTV News are convinced he wants one, given the political pressure he faces in the midterms.

One minister, who is not authorized to speak publicly on the issue, told CTV News it’s “now or maybe never” that a window exists to get Trump to make concessions to Canada on issues, particularly auto tariffs, that are not only dominating key senate races in places like Michigan, but have been identified as red lines by the prime minister.

Other red line issues include French language and culture, and Canada’s ability to trade with other countries. Two sources tell CTV News they expect Trump could move on the latter two, but autos remain the toughest negotiating issue.

Two ministers tell CTV News the message from “the centre” is “there’s a window” with the U.S. on these trade discussions, and to stay disciplined.

Two others were unsure Canada should hand Trump any kind of win in advance of the midterms. One of them noted the president has not stopped his rhetoric on Canada. As recently as last week, at a Michigan rally, Trump contended Canada has been “ripping off” the United States for years, without providing evidence.

Every minister who spoke to CTV News on background conveyed deep skepticism about a path to a broad “deal.” One said there are “too many free radicals” on the American negotiating team, especially when compared with the officials at the table during Trump’s first term.

Another minister said the “trust is gone.”

Trust between partners

That message was underscored by other people briefed on the state of talks who tied the breakdown in trust on both sides to the abrupt end to negotiations in August.

At a press conference after the U.S. imposed even more tariffs on Aug. 22, Prime Minister Mark Carney accused the White House of launching a trade “war” on Canada, and suggested America couldn’t be trusted because it sometimes signs in pencil.

Asked on Monday how he knows the president would sign in pen this time, Carney said he didn’t and wouldn’t say whether he trusts Trump.

Sources told CTV it remains unclear to the Canadian side whether the president is engaging them in earnest, or whether it’s just for show to appease angry midterm voters hoping for tariff relief.

On Wednesday, CTV News reported that U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra told an off-the-record business lunch on Tuesday that Canada could be blamed if results in Michigan and Maine go against the president next week.

The information was reported based on three sources with knowledge of the ambassador’s comments. CTV News is not identifying them as they were not authorized to disclose the confidential discussion.

The embassy said Hoekstra’s comments were taken out of context but declined to elaborate on what that additional context was.

One of the sources who spoke with CTV News said the private remarks show the difficult position Canada is in. Even if a deal is made, officials don’t know if they could trust it or how long it would last. On the flip side, if they don’t strike a deal, things could get worse.

At the same business lunch, Hoekstra also played down the prospects of reaching a deal this week. Two sources said he told the gathering that anyone hoping for an imminent deal would likely be disappointed.

A spokesperson for the U.S. embassy declined to comment “on private conversations.”

On Parliament Hill Wednesday, CTV News asked Carney why Canada was willing to entertain a deal with the United States, when Trump’s delegates were setting Canada up to take blame for midterm losses.

“We think there’s are deals that are in the best interests of Canada first and foremost, but also are in the interests of the United States. That’s always been the case,” Carney said.

“We’ve been consistent. If those deals present themselves, we will pursue them. But we’re not at that position right now.”

Ministers also conceded to CTV News selling a deal to Canadians will be as one put it, “next to impossible” as little to no preconditioning is being done with the public about the tariffs that Ottawa would have to agree to in any deal.

Canada’s top trade negotiator Janice Charette has warned business audiences that the tariffs are here to stay even if a deal is struck, but the same point has not been widely made with voters.

Multiple sources tell CTV News it was commerce secretary Howard Lutnick who initiated the talks last week, with one call lasting three hours. His presence in this round of talks is focused on the application of 232 tariffs on things like steel, aluminum and autos. Those tariffs are under his purview.

Lutnick was a chaotic force toward the end of negotiations in August, and sources at the time on the Canadian side said his last minute demands of Canada are part of the reason those talks fell apart. Three sources briefed on the state of current negotiations said they don’t trust Lutnick.

items._ogDesc: Canada and the European Union appear to be dropping the "associate member" term.
items.body:
OTTAWA — Canada and the European Union appear to be dropping the “associate member” term.

The controversial label when describing the future of the Canada-European Union relationship is not currently in the draft statement set to be released at this week’s summit between Canada and the 27-member bloc, CTV News has confirmed.

The draft statement for the summit is still being worked on, but two European sources confirm to CTV News the term “associate member” is currently not in the document.

The development was first reported by Politico on Wednesday.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen made headlines last month when she formally invited Prime Minister Mark Carney to take the Canada-EU relationship to the next level, at the time publicly floating the term “associate member” in a speech.

But, some EU member countries, led by Germany, have raised concerns about the label and have pushed back on it. The member countries contend they were not consulted on its use, though they support a closer relationship with Canada.

Both sources tell CTV News the draft statement for the summit has changed many times over the week and could change again.

This is a breaking news story. More details to come...

items.description: The federal Competition Bureau says that a proposed Air Canada and United Airlines arrangement could harm competition on 10 routes between Canada and the U.S., costing consumers millions of dollars in airfare.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[A United airlines plane sits near the terminal, Wednesday, November 17, 2021 in Ottawa.  (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Adrian Wyld</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: The federal Competition Bureau says that a proposed Air Canada and United Airlines arrangement could harm competition on 10 routes between Canada and the U.S., costing consumers millions of dollars in airfare.
items.body:
The federal Competition Bureau says that a proposed Air Canada and United Airlines arrangement could harm competition on 10 routes between Canada and the U.S., costing consumers millions of dollars in airfare.

The watchdog report was sent to Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon for review.

The 10 affected routes connect Toronto, Montreal, Ottawa and Vancouver with Chicago, Cleveland, Denver, Houston, New York, San Francisco and Washington.

The routes proposed are restricted by a 2012 consent agreement.

“The restrictions were put in place after the Bureau concluded that similar coordination between the airlines would substantially harm competition. The restrictions remain in force today,” the Competition Bureau said in a news release.

“The Bureau found that the proposed arrangement would eliminate an important source of competition between the airlines on these routes.”

The Canadian and American airlines account for all non-stop traffic on five of the 10 routes, the Bureau said, and have “significant combined market shares on the others.”

Transport Canada says the two airlines have operated under the Transborder Joint Business Arrangement (TBJBA), which allows them to work together on certain routes, since 2022.

“This includes coordination on joint pricing, inventory management, revenue sharing, and the exchange of competitively sensitive information,” Competition Bureau Canada said.

The airlines’ newly proposed arrangement includes an amended and restated version, which the Bureau said would “eliminate competition” on the 10 routes currently restricted.

“If the (agreement) is successfully rescinded, this would permit the Parties to coordinate on the (10) routes in the same manner contemplated by the TBJBA,” the Bureau said.

The proposed expansion would likely mean higher prices and “millions of dollars in consumer harm each year,” it stated, as the Air Canada-United arrangement could create monopoly or near-monopoly conditions on several routes.

“Competition between airlines helps keep fares lower and gives travellers more choice and better service,” said interim president Jeanne Pratt.

“Our review found that allowing Air Canada and United to coordinate on these routes would likely reduce competition on key Canada-U.S. routes and lead to higher prices for travellers.”

items._ogDesc: The Bank of Canada raised its key interest rate for the first time since July 2023 Wednesday to tamp down inflation, a hike Ontario Premier Doug Ford panned as 'a massive mistake.'
items.body:
The Bank of Canada raised its key interest rate for the first time since July 2023 Wednesday to tamp down inflation, a hike Ontario Premier Doug Ford panned as “a massive mistake.”

“Higher rates won’t get oil moving through the Strait of Hormuz or lower tariffs on Canadian businesses. They will only make life more expensive for Canadian families and workers, punishing them for something they can’t control,” Ford wrote in a tweet before the announcement was made this morning.

  • READ MORE: Bank of Canada raises key interest rate, says another hike possible

The bank increased its key policy rate by 25 basis points to 2.5 per cent, a move that was widely expected in the face of high oil prices and a rising interest rate, both brought on, in part, by the war in Iran and U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war.

Its inflation forecast for 2027 also rose to 3.1 per cent from the two per cent it had predicted in July. At the same time, the Canadian economy is expected to grow by one per cent in 2026 and two per cent in 2027, a “somewhat” stronger overall growth projection than what was forecast in the summer, the bank said.

As such, the bank said it may need to raise its interest rate again in the future.

“Against this backdrop, Governing Council decided to increase the policy rate to reduce the risk that continuing high energy prices spread broadly to the prices of other goods and services. There could be a need to increase the policy rate further, but given uncertainties, Governing Council agreed to proceed carefully,” officials said in a news release.

  • How to set CP24 as your preferred source on Google
  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

Ontario Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy, who is set to deliver the province’s fall economic statement on Thursday, had a more modest reaction to the expected interest rate jump, but said he understands Ford’s perspective.

“Who wouldn’t advocate for lower interest rates at a time when people are feeling the impacts of those higher interest rates? But at the end of the day, the Bank of Canada is an independent organization that has all the facts at their disposal, and keeping inflation in check is really important,” he told CTV News at an unrelated news conference before the rate hike was made official.

In simple terms, the Bank of Canada explains that, if the economy is growing too fast, it could lead to rising inflation. Raising the rate results in people and businesses paying higher interest on loans and mortgages, and discourages them from borrowing, reduces their spending and puts brakes on inflation.

“With higher rates, people tend to save more and spend less, slowing down the economy,” according to a post on their website.

Prior to Wednesday’s increase, the Bank of Canada hadn’t touched the interest rate since Oct. 29, 2025, when they dropped it by 25 basis points.

items.description: The Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate by 25 basis points to 2.5 per cent on Wednesday. Here is the text of the central bank’s decision.

items._ogDesc: The Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate by 25 basis points to 2.5 per cent on Wednesday. Here is the text of the central bank’s decision.
items.body:
OTTAWA — The Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate by 25 basis points to 2.5 per cent on Wednesday. Here is the text of the central bank’s decision:

The Bank of Canada today increased its target for the overnight rate by 25 basis points to 2.5 per cent, with the Bank Rate at 2.75 per cent and the deposit rate at 2.45 per cent.

Since the July Monetary Policy Report, global economic activity has remained resilient, despite higher energy prices. In the United States, the economy continues to grow at a robust pace, supported by consumer spending and AI-related investment. Growth in the euro area has been resilient and broad-based. After slowing in the second quarter, Chinese growth rebounded in the third quarter, owing to strength in exports and a pickup in fiscal spending. With persistently elevated oil prices and refinery margins, inflation has risen in most countries.

Given the ongoing resilience of the global economy, the Bank has revised up global GDP growth slightly to 3.1 per cent in 2026, while growth in 2027 and 2028 remains unchanged from the July projection at 3.2 per cent.

Global financial conditions have tightened since July. Advanced economy sovereign bond yields are higher. Equity and credit markets have been volatile due to uncertainty about the outlook for the AI sector. The Canadian dollar had weakened somewhat on U.S.-dollar strength but has since recovered to around 71 cents – the same as assumed in the July Report.

Growth picked up in Canada through the middle of the year. GDP growth was 3.3 per cent in the second quarter, and recent indicators point to growth of about two per cent in the third quarter. This is stronger than expected in the July Report. Consumer spending has been solid, even with slow population growth. Business investment rebounded, reflecting oil and gas sector activity and spending on machinery and equipment. Despite ongoing weakness in sectors affected by U.S. tariffs, exports overall have strengthened, owing to robust U.S. demand, higher energy production and increasing signs that businesses are adapting to the changing trade environment. The unemployment rate has been around 6.5 per cent for several months. A broad set of indicators continue to point to some excess supply in the economy.

Owing to new U.S. tariffs, growth is expected to slow in the fourth quarter of 2026, before picking up again in 2027. This rebound is supported by business investment, exports and fiscal measures. Consumption growth is expected to moderate and housing to remain relatively weak.

The Canadian economy is expected to grow one per cent in 2026, and two per cent in 2027 and 2028. This is a somewhat stronger overall growth projection than the July Report. This forecast is still subject to considerable uncertainty, particularly regarding Canada-U.S. trade relations.

Given persistently high oil prices, CPI inflation has been around three per cent since April and is expected to rise to about 3.5 per cent by the end of the year. Excluding gasoline, inflation was 2.2 per cent in September and measures of core inflation remain close to two per cent. But cost pressures are building, with high fuel prices raising the costs of production and transportation. Imported industrial and electronics input prices have also increased. While businesses have mostly absorbed higher input costs so far, Bank surveys suggest cost pass-through will increase over the next year. Near-term household and business inflation expectations have risen, while longer-term inflation expectations remain well anchored.

The conflict in the Middle East is now in its eighth month and there is no clear path to resolution. The combination of higher-for-longer energy prices and increased pass-through adds to the persistence of inflation in the projection. CPI inflation is expected to average three per cent in 2027, a percentage point above the July projection, then come down to two per cent in the middle of 2028. The main sources of uncertainty around this forecast are developments in the Middle East and businesses’ responses to cost pressures.

In the outlook, inflation is higher and more persistent than in the July Report. Growth has picked up this year and is expected to recover further. Against this backdrop, Governing Council decided to increase the policy rate to reduce the risk that continuing high energy prices spread broadly to the prices of other goods and services. There could be a need to increase the policy rate further, but given uncertainties, Governing Council agreed to proceed carefully. The Bank remains committed to maintaining Canadians’ confidence in price stability.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 28, 2026.

items.body:
OTTAWA — OTTAWA - The Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate by 25 basis points to 2.5 per cent. It’s the first hike since July 2023. The central bank wants to control inflation by reducing the risk that high fuel prices could spill over and seep into the overall economy.

In its October Monetary Policy Report, the BOC said the rise in energy prices and uncertainty surrounding Canada’s trade relationship with the United States are the two biggest risks to increasing costs of living.

In its report, the BOC said that high energy costs have not yet spread broadly to other prices, but “cost pressures are building and that businesses anticipate passing on more of their increased costs to customers.”

Inflation is currently at 3.1 per cent.

Tiff Macklem, the central bank’s governor, said that the outlook for inflation has “deteriorated” since the BOC’s July report.

“With the outlook for inflation substantially higher and the economy showing resilience, an increase in the policy rate is needed to reduce the risk that elevated energy prices could spill over and become generalized inflation,” Macklem said in prepared remarks during a Wednesday morning news conference.

  • Text of the Bank of Canada’s latest policy interest rate decision

The governor said that the persistent war in the Middle East means global oil prices will remain higher for longer and continue to hit Canadians at the gas pump while increasing costs for many businesses.

Eight months after the United States and Israel launched a war against Iran, the price of Brent crude is averaging $124.96 per barrel in October. The price of oil per barrel is about $35 more than in July.

Of the consumer-facing businesses surveyed by the central bank, 60 per cent expect to pass costs on to customers in the next 12 months.

The worrisome inflation outlook is buoyed by better-than-expected growth in the Canadian economy.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

The BOC said that growth increased in Canada through the middle of the year, reaching 3.3 per cent in the second quarter, but is expected to slow to 2 per cent in the third quarter.

Macklem said that growth can be attributed to “solid consumer spending” despite slow population increases. The governor said business investment has also rebounded, primarily led by activity in the oil and gas sector and spending on machinery and equipment.

“Despite ongoing weakness in sectors affected by US tariffs, exports overall have strengthened, bolstered by robust US demand, higher energy production and increasing signs that businesses are adapting to the changing trade environment,” Macklem said.

Macklem warned that the fourth quarter will likely show slower growth as “new US tariffs weigh on activity.”

The bank’s monetary report also pointed out the unemployment rate has hovered around 6.5 per cent in recent months, which suggests that it is “more difficult than usual for the unemployed to find work.”

After a decline in the next few months, the BOC projects that the economy will bounce back in 2027.

But Macklem said that, looking ahead, there was less scope for monetary accommodation with increasing inflation risks.

“There could be a need to raise the policy rate further, but given the uncertainties we will proceed carefully.”

items._ogDesc: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.5%, forecasting elevated inflation into 2028 as higher costs keep housing activity weak and push shelter inflation higher.
items.body:
Canada’s central bank raised its key policy rate as it tries to tame rising inflation. The Bank of Canada (BoC) hiked its overnight rate 25 basis points to 2.5% this morning, its first hike in over 3 years. In the accompanying report, the BoC warns of elevated inflation into mid-2028. Higher input and financing costs will also keep housing activity weak while boosting shelter inflation.

Canadian Inflation Isn’t Expected To Return To Target Until 2028

The BoC sees elevated inflation into 2028. The latest forecast from the central bank shows CPI inflation above 3% through Q3 2027. That’s roughly a point higher than they anticipated in their July report. It isn’t expected to return to their 2% target rate until mid-2028. While elevated inflation has largely been confined to energy and related categories, the Bank expects those pressures to spread over the next year.

High energy prices are spreading into production, transportation, and imports. Businesses have absorbed much of the increase so far, but expect to pass more on to consumers over the next 12 months, warns the BoC. Even after energy inflation turns negative in late 2027, earlier cost increases will continue to work their way through supply chains and boost prices.

Source: Bank of Canada.

Canadian Housing Investment Forecast To Lag The Economy

Higher rates are seen putting a drag on one of the country’s biggest components of GDP—housing investment. Residential investment primarily consists of spending on new home construction and substantial renovation. This sector is seen averaging less than 1% growth in 2027 and 2028. In contrast, GDP growth is expected to be roughly 2% for both years. The whole economy isn’t expected to slow, but housing will underperform.

Weak demand and high input costs are the reasons they cite. A lack of affordability, slow population growth, and rising borrowing costs are seen hitting the brakes on the demand side. Meanwhile, higher energy costs and imported input costs will make construction more expensive, throttling building activity.

Weak Housing Activity Isn’t Expected To Slow Rising Shelter Costs

Weak housing investment isn’t expected to slow shelter service inflation. It’s forecast to rise from just over 1% at the end of 2026 to 2% in 2027, and remain near that level into 2028. Higher material, equipment, construction, and maintenance costs are seen as the primary driver. Rising borrowing costs are expected to add further upward pressure. Rent inflation is seen as one of the few moderating factors for shelter, but it only partially offsets the other factors.

The impact on home prices isn’t clear, but higher expenses and weak demand aren’t bullish. At the same time, weak activity doesn’t automatically lead to affordability improvements.

The BoC report leaves an inflationary issue untouched: how government-backed construction spending supports higher input costs. Large projects compete for workers, resources, equipment, and land—even as private housing demand weakens. That spending can limit the disinflationary relief normally associated with a slowdown, leaving input costs elevated despite weak qualified demand.

items.description: Macklem warns oil price shock and Middle East conflict demand a policy response
items.content: <p>Macklem warns oil price shock and Middle East conflict demand a policy response</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639288017115537128.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Macklem warns oil price shock and Middle East conflict demand a policy response
items.body:
The Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate by 25 basis points to 2.5% on October 28, its first increase since July 2023, as Governor Tiff Macklem declared the central bank's commitment to price stability in "this period of global upheaval," anchoring the decision in a Middle East oil shock and unsettled Canada-US trade relations.

Speaking alongside Senior Deputy Governor Carolyn Rogers in Ottawa, Macklem identified two developments that had shifted the Bank's calculus since July 2026: a deteriorating inflation outlook, with oil prices expected to "remain higher for longer" as the Middle East conflict persisted, and a stronger domestic recovery despite US tariff pressure.

"We are mindful that uncertainty is still elevated," he said.

"Developments in the Middle East and Canada-US trade relations both remain fluid."

Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation has held near 3% since April and is projected to reach roughly 3.5% by year-end, with the 2% target not expected until mid-2028.

CPI excluding gasoline remains at 2.2% and core inflation sits near 2%.

"The longer energy prices remain high, the more likely it is these costs will spill over to consumer prices more broadly," Macklem said.

Oil, trade tensions, and the inflation risk that tipped the Bank's hand

Governing Council weighed that risk against solid economic data. Gross domestic product (GDP) grew 3.3% in the second quarter, with preliminary indicators pointing to about 2% growth in the third quarter, per the Bank of Canada's October 2026 Monetary Policy Report.

The unemployment rate has held near 6.5%, and full-year 2026 GDP growth is forecast at just 1% as US tariffs weigh on activity.

Not all forecasters agreed the moment called for action.Stéfane Marion, chief economist at National Bank of Canada (NBC) in Montréal, told the Mortgage Professionals Canada (MPC) conference in Calgary last week that core data argued for patience.

"Core inflation is still at 2%," he said.

"I don't think that the Bank of Canada should be hiking [on October 28] and if they do hike, they can't be too aggressive."

What the hike means for mortgage brokers

For Canadian mortgage brokers, the decision reshapes client conversations immediately.

Variable-rate mortgage holders will see payments rise as lenders' prime rates move from 4.45% to 4.70%, a shift that renewal discussions and rate-path strategy had been building toward all year, and Wednesday's announcement intensifies the pressure.

Leah Zlatkin, a Toronto-based licensed mortgage broker and expert commentator with LowestRates.ca, said one move is unlikely to be the last.

"If there is a hike, I do think it's going to be a cycle," Zlatkin said.

TD Bank economist Marc Ercolao, speaking from Toronto, said Macklem had telegraphed the outcome weeks earlier.

"It was Bank of Canada Governor Macklem's remarks a couple of weeks ago that likely tipped the scales towards today's decision to hike," Ercolao said.

"The Bank of Canada said it does not see a clear offramp to the conflict in the Middle East and is increasingly worried about the risks to inflation."

Governing Council signalled caution on what comes next, stopping short of any firm commitment to further action.

"Looking ahead, Governing Council agreed we would take future decisions one meeting at a time," Macklem said.

"There could be a need to raise the policy rate further, but given the uncertainties, we will proceed carefully."

The Bank's next rate decision is December 9.

items.title: AI tools may make women sound less sophisticated at work
items.description: A new study raises questions about how AI-generated writing could shape perceptions of professionalism and competence
items.content: <p>A new study raises questions about how AI-generated writing could shape perceptions of professionalism and competence</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/035/0394_639283811160256015.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: A new study raises questions about how AI-generated writing could shape perceptions of professionalism and competence
items.body:
Two people can ask an AI chatbot for the same workplace email and get noticeably different results, depending on little more than their choice of words.

That’s the finding at the center of new research from Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore. Researchers tested four widely used chatbots, GPT-4, Llama, Gemma and Mistral, with prompts for workplace emails, job applications and resignation letters.

When they rewrote the prompts to include language more commonly associated with women, such as hedges like “maybe” and “I think,” collective phrasing like “we” and “our team,” and expressive adjectives like “lovely” and “wonderful,” the responses came back less complex, at a lower grade level and less formal.

Katherine Van Koevering, an inaugural postdoctoral fellow at the university’s Data Science and AI Institute and the study’s lead author, said the size of the difference surprised the team.

“The headline finding, of course, is that when we rewrote prompts asking for workplace communication using more women-associated linguistic features, the model output was of a lower complexity level, lower grade level, I believe less formal,” Van Koevering said. “It looked surprisingly different.”

Anjalie Field, the study’s senior author and a Johns Hopkins computer scientist in Baltimore who studies ethics and discrimination in AI, said earlier research has examined bias in what the models produce.

“There’s been a lot less research that really focuses on the perspective of people using these models and how models perform for different groups of people or even different individuals,” Field said.

Ruling out mirroring

One obvious question is whether the models were simply echoing the style of the person writing the prompt. To test for that, the researchers measured the complexity of each prompt and compared it with the complexity of the response.

“We would measure the complexity of the prompt, and then we compare that to the complexity of the output,” Van Koevering said. “That would tell us how much of this is mirroring versus the AI picking up on something else.”

“Mirroring only accounted for, I think, a third or less, even at our highest level of mirroring,” she added.

In most cases the share was much smaller. At the highest level, mirroring explained about a third of the complexity differences, which generally isn’t enough to undermine the statistical significance of the findings.

The effect appeared in all four tools, though its strength varied by model.

“I wouldn’t say it was exactly the same, but the significance of the results held for every model we tested,” Van Koevering said.

What it could mean for workplace writing

With mirroring explaining only part of the difference, attention turns to what the results mean at work.

“Anyone who uses this kind of language, who uses things like hedges or expressive adjectives, could be getting outputs from models that are less sophisticated, less complex, and less formal,” Field said.

“If you prompt a model with this kind of language and you then take that output and send it to your colleague, that’s going to reflect on you and how they think about you,” she added.

The researchers also asked an AI to compare outputs from woman-associated and man-associated prompts and say which seemed more authoritative and competent.

“[The AI] chose the output for the male sociolinguistic feature prompts most of the time,” Van Koevering said.

She said there’s some suggestion that the effect extends beyond how sophisticated the writing sounds to how competent and authoritative it comes across.

Van Koevering said the pattern may extend well beyond gender, too.

“In theory, this works on any kind of linguistic differences,” she said. “If you type with British spelling, maybe it responds to you differently. If you use slang, maybe it responds to you differently.”

The team also tested whether including a traditionally male or female name changed the response. It had virtually no effect, according to the Johns Hopkins release.

Other research has looked at how AI systems treat gender in workplace settings. In a University of Washington study of AI resume screening that its authors summarized in an April 2025 Brookings Institution article, men’s and women’s names were selected at equal rates in only 37% of 27 resume screening tests across three language models and nine occupations. HRD America has also reported on University of Chicago research showing that women were less likely than men to use ChatGPT in the same occupation, and on an International Labour Organization warning that generative AI could affect women’s jobs more than men’s.

What companies and workers can do

Asked what organizations should do with the new findings, Field said flagging the issue to staff is one option.

That would mean providing guidance that many workers say they haven’t received. In a May 2026 survey of 1,020 employees by career platform Resume Now, 41% said their employer has given them no tools, training or guidance for using AI, HRD America reported.

For individual workers, Field said one way to handle it is to be careful about how they prompt a model and to check that the style and tone of the output match what they want to send. She said adding instructions about the desired tone to a prompt is another option, though the team didn’t explicitly test it.

Van Koevering said workers can test the effect themselves.

“Write it how you would imagine writing it, and then make up some personas in your head and write it different ways and just see the difference,” she said.

She said the drawback is the extra time it takes to rework writing people have probably already spent a lot of time on.

Field said she doesn’t like these workarounds as a long-term solution because they put the burden on the user. In her view, the models should be trained to pay attention to the tone and style each type of request calls for, however it’s phrased.

“That’s not a solution for HR managers. That’s what the technologists should be working on,” Field said.

In the meantime, the researchers’ suggestions come down to awareness and testing. Employers can make sure staff know that the way a request is phrased may change the tone of what an AI tool writes, and workers can check that tone before a message goes out.

Until the models themselves change, the findings suggest the same request can still come back sounding different depending on how it’s worded.

The Bank of Canada raised its target for the overnight rate by 25 basis points on Wednesday, bringing it to 2.5% and marking the first increase since July 0f 2023.

The Bank Rate now sits at 2.75%, and the deposit rate at 2.45%.

Inflation is running higher and longer than the Bank projected in July. CPI inflation has hovered around 3% since April, and the Bank expects it to climb to about 3.5% by the end of the year, largely because of persistently high oil prices.

Take gasoline out and the numbers look calmer. Inflation excluding gas was 2.2% in September, and core measures remain close to 2%. The Bank is more worried about where costs are heading. High fuel prices are raising production and transportation costs, imported industrial and electronics inputs have become more expensive, and Bank surveys suggest businesses will pass more of those costs on to customers over the next year.

The conflict in the Middle East is now in its eighth month with no clear path to resolution. The Bank expects CPI inflation to average 3% in 2027, a full percentage point above its July projection, before easing to 2% in the middle of 2028.

Governing Council said the hike is meant to reduce the risk that high energy prices spread into the prices of other goods and services. It said further increases may be needed, but that it would proceed carefully given the uncertainty.

The economy has outperformed expectations. GDP grew 3.3% in the second quarter, and recent indicators point to about 2% growth in the third, both stronger than the Bank anticipated. Consumer spending held up despite slow population growth, and business investment rebounded on oil and gas activity and machinery and equipment spending. Unemployment has held around 6.5% for several months.

New US tariffs are expected to slow growth in the fourth quarter. The Bank projects the economy will grow 1% in 2026 and 2% in both 2027 and 2028, a somewhat stronger outlook than July’s, though Canada-US trade relations remain a major source of uncertainty.

Business investment, exports and fiscal measures are expected to drive the 2027 rebound. Housing, however, isn’t on that list. The Bank expects it to remain relatively weak, with consumption growth moderating as well.

items.description: Central bank moves rates higher as inflation fears rise
items.content: <p>Central bank moves rates higher as inflation fears rise</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639287915827940101.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Central bank moves rates higher as inflation fears rise
items.body:
The Bank of Canada has hiked its benchmark rate for the first time since July 2023 amid rising fears about the national inflation outlook.

The central bank said on Wednesday morning it was raising that trendsetting interest rate by 25 basis points to a level of 2.50%, ending its long wait-and-see approach on the rate question.

Major Canadian lenders are expected to increase their prime rates following the decision. Variable mortgage rates, as well as home equity lines of credit (HELOCs), typically rise and fall in tandem with Bank of Canada moves.

Odds of a rate jump by the BoC had risen in recent weeks as fuel costs continue to surge, mainly because of the ongoing US-Iran war.

The overall consumer price index (CPI) climbed only modestly month over month in September (to 3.1%, up by 0.1%), but the Bank’s move will be viewed as a pre-emptive bid to stave off the threat of higher energy costs spilling into other sectors.

The hike is the Bank’s first step off the sidelines in 2026. It’s held rates steady through the year to date as it weighs a sluggish national economy against growing concerns on the inflation front.

While the Bank kept rate hikes on ice until today, fixed mortgage rates rose steadily in September because of the upward trajectory of five-year Government of Canada bond yields.  

BoC governor Tiff Macklem will face the media at about 10:30 a.m. ET this morning and could give some indication of whether further rate hikes are likely in the months ahead.

What’s next for the BoC?

For now, it looks unlikely that the central bank will embark on a series of steep hikes similar to the last time it started raising rates.

In March 2022, the BoC bumped rates 25 basis points higher after nearly two years at rock-bottom lows of 0.25% – and that was a sign of things to come, with its policy rate spiking by a further 450 basis points in the 16 months following that move.

This time around, the weakness of the Canadian economy and the continuing negative impact of trade tensions with the US mean lenders and financial markets are pricing in only mild further increases by the Bank.

What the decision means for the housing market

For the housing market, it remains to be seen whether today’s decision will push potential homebuyers onto the sidelines.

Housing and mortgage market watchers had been increasingly anticipating some rate increase by the BoC in recent weeks – but even the expectation of hikes hadn’t compelled many would-be buyers to rush into the market to secure mortgage rates at their current level.

The Bank has one further rate decision in store for 2026, with that announcement set for December 9.

items.title: Mortgage market ‘still recovering’ from BoC’s COVID rate cuts, says lender president
items.description: The mortgage industry could be facing a much different environment if the central bank hadn’t decided to slash rates to record lows in 2020, says MIC executive
items.content: <p>The mortgage industry could be facing a much different environment if the central bank hadn’t decided to slash rates to record lows in 2020, says MIC executive</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639287200172090755.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: The mortgage industry could be facing a much different environment if the central bank hadn’t decided to slash rates to record lows in 2020, says MIC executive
items.body:
The Bank of Canada is gearing up for what many pundits say could be the start of a new rate-hiking cycle – but the housing and mortgage markets are still dealing with the impact of its COVID-era rate policy even years later, according to the president of a prominent mortgage lender.

The central bank slashed its benchmark rate to a rock-bottom 0.25% at the onset of the pandemic, helping cause a homebuying frenzy as mortgage rates plunged and borrowers jumped into the market.

A series of rapid rate hikes in 2022 and 2023 put a halt to that housing boom, but Westboro Mortgage Investment Corporation president Derek Serra (pictured top) told Canadian Mortgage Professional he still sees the negative effects of the low-rate era seeping through.

“I think that we’re still kind of recovering from the decision to have lowered interest rates during COVID. And the outcome of that decision sparked such an incredible inflationary time for Canadians,” he said. “I’ve been in banking for 30 years, and I’ve always seen Canadians using the equity in their home as an opportunity for them to pay for their kids’ education.

“There was almost a kind of a familiarity or a consistency with expecting a little bit of growth in the value of your home. And so when these inflationary times came through COVID, which was triggered by the very low interest rates, the average Canadian saw rapid increases in their property values – which at the time sparked them to do more than what they usually do without, necessarily, the kind of long-term perspective.”

‘There was the opinion that rates… would stay low for a long time’

In 2025 and 2026, scores of mortgages originated during the pandemic have come up for renewal, almost always at much higher rates compared with five years prior.

That trend is part of the reason mortgage delinquencies are climbing, with Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) indicating on Tuesday it doesn’t expect the rise of mortgage arrears in Ontario to end until the middle of next year.

Serra suggested the Bank of Canada’s decision to dramatically cut rates in 2020 might have been the wrong one looking back.

“There was also kind of the opinion that rates would be low and stay low for a long time, and obviously that shifted for a variety of reasons,” he said. “And now we’re seeing the outcome of that decision.

“In hindsight, it’s always easy to look back and question, but you wonder if maybe we hadn’t dropped rates at the time, we would have felt more pain then – but it would have been a different kind of 2026 now.”

As the central bank embarked on a rate-hiking spree in 2022 and 2023, industry and expert opinion was divided on whether governor Tiff Macklem had misled Canadians by suggesting that interest rates wouldn’t be rising anytime soon.

Macklem told the House of Commons standing committee on finance in November 2020 that Canadians “can be confident that borrowing costs are going to remain very low for a very long time” – but within less than three years, the BoC’s benchmark rate had shot up by 475 basis points.

Critics said that reassurance may have convinced Canadians the time was right to purchase a home without factoring in higher costs down the line. Macklem’s defenders, on the other hand, pointed to unexpected developments including Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the further supply chain snarls caused by the emergence of the Omicron COVID variant.

Appraisal challenges continue in higher-rate environment

As well as causing challenges for borrowers at renewal time, the post-pandemic march toward higher rates poured cold water on a red-hot housing market. In that environment, appraisal challenges have arisen because there are so few transactions in many cities to judge whether or how far a property’s value may have fallen.

Serra, though, pointed to some recent cause for optimism on that front. “The good news is we’ve seen a little bit of increase in the past four weeks in purchase transactions, and that is a really good sign,” he said.

“It’s an early indicator… but as we see purchase transactions, even if they’re at lower values, we’re able to now properly assess where the market’s at. If you’re living in a community where there haven’t been any sales, it’s very difficult to substantiate the value of these properties, especially for clients who are looking for higher loan-to-values.”

items.description: Outlook remains mixed for property valuations, CRE financing
items.content: <p>Outlook remains mixed for property valuations, CRE financing</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639287837545548261.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Outlook remains mixed for property valuations, CRE financing
items.body:
Industrial landlords in the Greater Toronto Area (GTA) are filling more space, but rents continue to fall, creating a mixed outlook for property valuations and commercial real estate financing.

Average asking net rents fell to $16.06 per square foot in the third quarter of 2026, down 4.8% from a year earlier, according to Avison Young's latest industrial market report. Meanwhile, vacancy declined to 2.6%, from 2.7% in the previous quarter and 3.2% a year earlier.

The gap between improving occupancy and falling rents matters for property owners seeking financing or refinancing, as stronger leasing does not necessarily mean higher rental income.

Despite the decline, GTA industrial rents remain 38% above levels recorded five years ago.

Demand for industrial space continued to grow, with net absorption reaching 2.2 million square feet during the quarter and 11.2 million square feet year to date. Logistics and distribution companies led leasing activity, with manufacturers, technology and pharmaceutical firms, consumer goods businesses, and retailers also contributing.

Major transactions included LG Electronics' 980,800-square-foot lease in King City, Brewers Retail's 679,400-square-foot lease in Milton and Amazon's 246,000-square-foot lease in Brampton.

However, leasing conditions varied across the GTA. The North recorded the lowest vacancy rate at 2.0% and the highest average asking net rent at $17.63 per square foot. In contrast, vacancy in the East remained elevated at 5.0%, despite a slight quarterly decline.

GTA Central was the only region where vacancy increased, rising 20 basis points to 2.4%, while GTA West recorded the largest improvement, with vacancy falling 30 basis points to 2.6%. These differences highlight the importance of local market conditions when assessing industrial property income and valuations.

Beyond location, property specifications are also influencing tenant demand. Industrial buildings with clear heights of at least 30 feet commanded average asking net rents of $16.84 per square foot, compared with $14.86 for buildings with clear heights of 18 to 21 feet. Avison Young linked this preference to businesses seeking more efficient facilities to meet changing supply-chain needs.

Industrial construction has also slowed across the GTA, reflecting broader Canadian industrial development trends.

Space under construction fell to 5.9 million square feet across 28 buildings at the end of September, down from 10.8 million square feet in the previous quarter. Active construction represented just 0.6% of the GTA's existing industrial inventory.

Another 48 million square feet remained in the pre-construction pipeline, but only 1% had been pre-leased. Avison Young said the limited tenant commitments suggest developers remain cautious about advancing projects without sufficient demand. Earlier reporting on Canada's industrial construction pipeline also examined the slowdown in development activity.

The 1.3 million square feet completed during the quarter had a combined vacancy rate of 12% upon delivery.

Meanwhile, industrial property sale prices moved in the opposite direction to rents, rising to an average of $378 per square foot from $355 in the previous quarter.

items.title: Equity shortages threaten Canadian CRE refinancing in 2027
items.description: Debt remains available, but lenders favour stronger borrowers
items.content: <p>Debt remains available, but lenders favour stronger borrowers</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639287835999782539.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Debt remains available, but lenders favour stronger borrowers
items.body:
Canada's commercial real estate market is recovering, but a shortage of borrower equity could complicate refinancing in 2027 despite readily available debt financing, according to the Emerging Trends in Real Estate 2027 report from PwC Canada and the Urban Land Institute (ULI).

Commercial real estate investment reached $16.2 billion in the second quarter of 2026, its highest level since early 2022, according to CBRE. Canadian investors' willingness to buy property has also reached its strongest level in 15 years.

Despite the recovery, lenders remain selective, favouring established borrowers and properties with stable income. With a wave of commercial mortgages due for refinancing in 2027, securing enough equity could be a bigger challenge for some borrowers than obtaining debt.

The report points to growing use of preferred equity and mezzanine debt to fill the gap between senior loans and borrowers' available capital. According to Lee-Anne Kovacs, national real estate leader at PwC Canada, these financing options could help property owners refinance existing debt or raise additional funds.

"Optimism is returning to Canadian real estate, but it must be earned. We are seeing clearer signs that the market is turning a corner, with opportunities emerging across asset classes and regions. The organizations best positioned for the next cycle will be those that remain selective, move with conviction and address the constraints standing between improving conditions and real opportunity,” Kovacs said.

The uneven recovery is particularly clear in Toronto, where the struggling condominium market contrasts with stronger demand for other commercial properties.

Greater Toronto Area pre-construction condominium sales fell 80% year over year in the second quarter of 2026, according to Urbanation, while completed, unsold developer inventory reached a record 5,001 units.

Meanwhile, CBRE reported downtown Toronto Class AAA office vacancy of just 2.6%, while Colliers placed the city's industrial vacancy rate at 2.2%, the lowest in Canada. These differences show why property type and rental income remain important considerations in financing decisions, even within the same city.

"The GTA's real estate market is moving at different speeds. Industrial and premium office show signs of recovery, while condominiums remain challenged. Purpose-built rental is supporting construction despite difficult project economics. Long-term investment opportunities remain, but realizing them requires patient capital and sustained housing delivery to prevent today's slowdown from creating future supply gaps and renewed pressure on housing affordability,” said Richard Joy, executive director at Urban Land Institute, Toronto.

Elsewhere, Calgary and Edmonton are attracting investor interest, supported by stronger economic growth forecasts. Calgary ranks first among Canadian markets to watch for 2027, with real GDP growth projected at 3.4%, according to Signal49. Edmonton is expected to grow by 3.0%, with continued interest in smaller industrial properties.

Across Canada, the report identifies senior housing, retail and industrial properties as the leading investment opportunities for 2027, although each comes with different risks.

Demand for senior housing is growing with Canada's ageing population. Cushman & Wakefield estimates that nearly 200,000 additional rental units will be needed over the next decade, although staffing and operating requirements add complexity.

Retail properties are benefiting from limited new supply and renewed tenant demand. Industrial investors, meanwhile, favour small- and mid-bay facilities, while larger properties face greater risk when they depend on a single major tenant.

items.title: Municipalities await future of housing law after change in B.C. government
items.description: The B.C. Conservatives have promised to return authority to local governments to determine where housing density will go.
items._ogDesc: The B.C. Conservatives have promised to return authority to local governments to determine where housing density will go.
items.body:
Local councils returning to work in the wake of the municipal election are waiting to see what a new B.C. Conservative government does with provincial housing legislation that forced them to redo their bylaws and official community plans.

During the campaign, the party promised to return authority to local governments to determine where housing density will go.

The promise was a step back from its threat a couple of years ago to repeal Bill 44, which was enacted by the NDP government in 2023 to stimulate housing starts.

The legislation required municipalities to amend their bylaws by mid 2024 to allow four to six units on single-family and duplex lots, effectively up-zoning most of the province.

It also outlawed public hearings for development projects that conform to official community plans.

The latter raised the ire of many residents, who felt they no longer had any say on what was being built around them.

Victoria Mayor Marianne Alto, who was re-elected for a second term, said the city is waiting to see if the next government has “profoundly different directives.”

She said the 2023 provincial changes fit well with the city’s existing approach to housing development.

“Frankly our own agendas were more assertive than that anyway,” she said, adding they also didn’t have any problem with the province setting housing targets.

“We knew we’d exceed them, which we have.”

The most recent data available shows the City of Victoria had issued 2,359 occupancy permits for new homes by late fall 2025, well ahead of the goal of 1,425. Victoria’s target is to issue 4,902 occupancy permits by 2028.

Alto said the city will continue on its current path, including policies geared at producing more affordable housing, until told otherwise.

She noted that the incoming provincial government has suggested it intends to push for more affordable housing. “I suspect that they’re probably going to look at ways to do that,” she said.

Across the border in Saanich, the Bill 44 changes and loss of public hearings were a big issue for many residents.

Outgoing Saanich Mayor Dean Murdock said revising the official community plan and zoning rules to accommodate what is called small-scale multi-unit housing — like townhouses and multi-plexes — was a lot of work for district staff.

Undoing it would also require a “significant” amount of work if that’s the direction the new provincial government chooses to go, he said.

The district also created policies to guide the application process around small-scale multi-unit housing, updating its building permit language. “Those things would all have to be revised,” he said.

“This could be a major diversion in terms of priorities that a future council may set.”

Murdock said new governments are typically “allergic to the policies of their predecessors,” so while they may recognize the value in creating more family-suitable housing, they’re likely to just rip apart the current legislation.

“The issues around housing availability and affordability are not going away, and they will be very much a pressure on a Conservative government, just as it has been for an NDP government,” he said.

The Conservatives have said they will remove red tape around housing construction, review the costs that slow it down, shorten approval times and overhaul the B.C. Energy Step Code, which sets energy-efficiency requirements for new buildings.

Mike Drummond, chief executive of the Urban Development Institute, the voice of the development industry, said blanket up-zoning had unintended consequences, such as making land assembly more difficult. “In the end, we believe municipalities should have more flexibility on where added density goes.”

Drummond is also keen to see the new government tackle some of the problems stalling projects, including building code changes and permanently removing the expansion of the PST to professional services such as architectural and engineering work. The proposed expansion, which was supposed to come into effect Oct. 1, was paused by the previous NDP government

Casey Edge, executive director of the Victoria Residential Builders Association, said he would like the provincial government to limit the cost charges that municipalities can set for developers. Such charges, which are collected for water, sanitary sewers, drainage, parks and transportation upgrades to service new development, add thousands to the cost of a home, Edge said.

Last term, Victoria council considered more than doubling the fees developers pay toward infrastructure needed to support new housing, including roads, water and sewer systems, drainage and parks.

Edge said the government should also look at replacing the Step Code, enforcing interpretation of its own building code and holding municipalities accountable for permit delays.

“There should be reasonable timelines for permits,” he said. “There is no reason a permit for a new single-family home takes two weeks in one municipality and months in another municipality.”

items.description:
